content.title: About
content.content: Barbecue sauce is a thick, flavorful sauce made from tomatoes, vinegar, sugar, and spices, used for marinating, glazing, and serving with meat dishes, especially grilled and smoked foods. It has a sweet‑tart taste with a hint of smokiness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial barbecue sauce appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
Traditional recipes include tomato paste, brown sugar, vinegar, mustard, and aromatic spices such as paprika, garlic, and onion powder.
Different U.S. regions have their own styles: Kentucky sauces are more tomato‑based, while Texas versions are spicier and smokier.
Barbecue sauce is often used both as a marinade and as a finishing glaze to create a caramelized crust.
Gluten‑free and vegan versions exist, substituting honey with maple syrup or agave.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and spices provide lycopene and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Vinegar stimulates stomach acid production, aiding protein digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many sauces, barbecue sauce typically contains little fat when no oil is added.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: The tomato base supplies a modest amount of vitamin C, supporting the immune system.

items.title: Moderate sugar content
items.content: Sugar gives quick energy, but most commercial sauces have less sugar than sweet ketchup.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Some varieties contain a lot of added sugar, which can be problematic for diabetics or those watching weight.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Vinegar and salt make the sauce fairly salty; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Ingredients may include mustard, soy sauce, or dairy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial sauces often contain preservatives (e.g., sodium benzoate) that some sensitive individuals prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Use barbecue sauce as a marinade for chicken, pork, or beef, as a glaze during the last minutes of grilling, and as a dip for fries, veggie sticks, and burgers. It can also be mixed into salad dressings or incorporated into sauces for barbecue‑style dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in a tightly sealed jar in the refrigerator after opening. Unopened, it can be kept at room temperature for up to 12 months; once opened, use within 3‑4 weeks. Discard if mold, off‑color, or off‑smell appear.
